bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds Republicans’ “steep” losses or “election wipeout,” portraying Thune’s reelection as continuity despite a collapse in power and highlighting “MAGA” outrage; right-leaning coverage instead frames the same vote as a failed “mini-revolt” or rejected “post-election reckoning,” using “RINO” to signal conservatives’ doubts about Thune’s commitment to Trump-aligned priorities, including Senate rules, abortion, and the SAVE America Act.
Center coverage de-emphasizes ideological combat, stressing the closed-door procedure and failed delay effort.
All perspectives emphasize the minority transition, internal tensions, and Thune’s victory, reflecting wider divides over establishment continuity versus populist accountability.
summary: Senate Republicans reelected Majority Leader John Thune as their leader on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, despite internal pushback following widespread midterm losses.
Widespread election defeats that cost Republicans the Senate majority prompted a day of internal reckoning on Capitol Hill as lawmakers grappled with the party's direction.

The Senate held tense closed-door meetings over whether to delay leadership votes, while the House GOP leadership contest opened between Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan.

Republican lawmakers expressed deep frustrations over the election performance, with Rep Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, calling the closed-door meeting a "needed family discussion" to reevaluate the party's path forward.
Members aim to define their legislative agenda for the 120th Congress against incoming Democrats after what Thune described as a "tough night" in the midterm elections.
title: Source Icon

summary: On Tuesday, House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio as minority leader in a closed-door secret-ballot vote, defeating House Majority Leader Steve Scalise 106–73. Jordan will assume the role when the 120th Congress convenes in January.

Following heavy midterm losses in which Democrats flipped at least 44 seats, outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson announced he would not seek another leadership post. This opened a direct path for the 62-year-old firebrand to lead the diminished conference.

Jordan campaigned as a 'battle-tested' leader ready for aggressive oversight, contrasting sharply with Scalise's pitch emphasizing legislative experience and $67.9 million in midterm fundraising. The conference chose confrontation over continuity, signaling a shift in strategy.

Republicans also re-elected Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota as minority whip, defeating Rep. August Pfluger 103–36. The conference will hold additional elections for conference chair and other positions to complete its leadership team.

Jordan faces the challenge of uniting a historically small Republican conference while countering Democratic investigations of the Trump administration. He must position the party to reclaim nearly 50 lost seats by 2028, balancing aggressive oversight with appeals to swing voters.
title: GOP Taps Combative Jordan as Next House Minority Leader

bias: Left-Leaning coverage emphasizes the arrest, “counter-terror police,” and Russia-linked espionage while generally retaining “suspected,” though some wording amplifies the soldier’s status as “high-ranking.” Right-leaning coverage more sharply frames the case as insider betrayal, using “passing secrets,” “Russian spy,” and “betrayal of military oaths,” foregrounding military loyalty and classified-information risks.
Center coverage more consistently stresses “allegations,” legal provisions, and the ongoing investigation, occasionally adding broader security context.
The pivotal divide is whether access to sensitive information is portrayed as possible disclosure.
All perspectives highlight the 41-year-old’s arrest, allied cooperation, and Russia connection, reflecting wider debates over legal caution versus national-security threat.
summary: On Tuesday, British counter- terrorism police arrested a 41-year-old member of the Army from the United States near Gloucester, England, on suspicion of National Security Act 2023 offenses linked to Russia.

Counter Terrorism Policing led the investigation working with the FBI and United States military; FBI Director Kash Patel stated the arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is "of the utmost concern."
Officers are currently conducting searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, while the suspect remains in custody at a London police station as enquiries under the National Security Act continue.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans from Counter Terrorism Policing described the arrest as "significant", and the suspect is accused of violating two sections of the National Security Act for assisting a foreign intelligence service.

Authorities confirmed the investigation is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing operations as enquiries continue regarding the 41-year-old soldier's alleged espionage activities.
title: US army member arrested in UK over 'allegations of espionage' involving Russia

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the 0.4% October CPI rise as household distress—“affordability challenges,” consumers “hammered by high prices,” and voter “discontent”—while noting slower gasoline increases as limited relief and linking inflation to Democratic gains.

Right-Leaning coverage portrays the same figure as policy failure, using “surging” prices, “zero relief in sight,” “Trump economy,” and “Fed nightmare,” while stressing a likely or larger December hike, markets, and geopolitical explanations such as an Iran war.
Center coverage is more restrained, emphasizing missing shutdown-era comparisons and market probabilities.
All agree prices exceeded forecasts and rate pressure intensified, reflecting broader disputes over governance, economic blame, and consumer hardship.
summary: The BLS reported Tuesday that the consumer price index increased 0.4% in October, exceeding the 0.3% increase economists expected and signaling fresh warning signs for The Fed's inflation fight.
Last year's government shutdown prevented The Bureau from collecting sufficient data in October 2025, leaving no year-ago figures available for comparison in this month's report.
Stripping out volatile food and energy, core CPI increased 0.3% against a 0.2% forecast, while gas prices fell below $4 per gallon; Diesel prices, however, remained 70% higher than year-start.
Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller said earlier Tuesday that if core inflation rose 0.3% or higher, a 0.50% rate hike "should be considered" at December's meeting.
Inflation has not hit The Fed's 2% target since early 2021, keeping the central bank on track to raise interest rates next month amid persistent price pressures.
title: U.S. Inflation Rose 0.4% in October, More Than Expected

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Proposition 40 as a “war on wealth,” stressing billionaires’ $300-million-plus campaign spending, healthcare funding, and a “blow to the left,” while right-leaning coverage calls its defeat “dashing liberal dreams,” portraying the tax as “nonsense,” unaffordability-inducing, and a trigger for capital flight.

The pivotal divide is whether a one-time 5% levy on billionaires represents progressive healthcare investment or economically damaging overreach; Newsom’s warning that wealthy residents might leave receives greater weight on the right, while the left emphasizes inequality and campaign divisions.
Center coverage presents a political “win” and future policy test.
All agree voters rejected the measure after a costly campaign, reflecting wider disputes over taxation, inequality, and government’s economic role.
summary: California voters rejected Proposition 40, a ballot measure proposing a 5% tax on assets for residents with net worths exceeding $1.1 billion to fund healthcare.

Critics, including outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom and gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, argued the tax would prompt wealthy residents to flee; many progressives opposed it as a one-time levy rather than permanent policy.

According to ad-tracking firm AdImpact, opponents outspent supporters 250 to 1 in late October, backed by coalitions including the California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, Planned Parenthood, and Google co-founder Sergey Brin.

While Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., campaigned for the measure, the outcome reveals sharp divisions among Democrats regarding party direction heading into the 2028 presidential contest.
title: Californians reject wealth tax for billionaires

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the 211–204 referral as Republicans “blocking,” “quashing,” or “shielding” Hegseth from scrutiny over eight articles alleging unauthorized military action, an “illegal war,” and abuses of power; right-leaning accounts portray a “lone Republican” Massie’s push as a partisan “farce” that “miserably failed,” emphasizing Democratic absences, GOP unity, and Hegseth’s supposed “exoneration.” The pivotal divide is whether committee referral represents obstruction or ordinary procedure—and whether it establishes accountability delayed or vindication achieved.
Center coverage stresses the procedural “reprieve” and institutional uncertainty.

All perspectives acknowledge the vote halted immediate impeachment , left Hegseth in office, and could be revisited, reflecting broader disputes over executive power, war-making, and partisan loyalty.
summary: On Tuesday, the House voted 211-204 to refer impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, effectively stalling the effort. Republican Representative Thomas Massie led the push to remove the Pentagon chief.

Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment alleging Hegseth committed 'high crimes and misdemeanors,' including unauthorized military actions in Iran and Yemen. He also alleges Hegseth ordered 'extrajudicial killings' of at least 240 people in the Caribbean and Pacific.

While Hegseth dismissed the allegations as 'a political spectacle driven by ego and resentment,' 11 Democrats missed the ballot citing traffic incidents. President Trump celebrated the outcome as an 'exoneration' on his Truth Social feed.

Incoming House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries recently said Democrats would 'run Pete Hegseth out of town,' signaling the Pentagon chief will remain a target of congressional investigations and potential future impeachment efforts.

Democrats are set to take control of Congress on January 3, potentially reviving impeachment proceedings against Hegseth. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan noted, 'You should show up and do your job,' emphasizing accountability.
title: GOP House rejects Hegseth impeachment effort

bias: Left-Leaning coverage emphasizes procedure and delay—Momeni’s denied new-trial request, the passage of years, and “finally” receiving sentence—while right-leaning framing narrows attention to punishment and public safety, using charged terms such as “killer,” “brutal,” “murder,” and “learns his fate.” The pivotal divide is whether the story centers on post-conviction legal process or violent accountability: left coverage foregrounds the court’s procedural steps, whereas the right highlights the stabbing and condemnation.

Center coverage adds context—three wounds, a kitchen knife, the Bay Bridge, and the case’s celebrity “saga.” All emphasize the conviction and 16-years-to-life sentence, reflecting shared legal focus amid differing institutional and cultural priorities.
summary: On Tuesday, San Francisco Superior Court Judge Alexandra Gordon sentenced Nima Momeni to 16 years to life in prison for the 2023 second-degree murder of Cash App founder Bob Lee , rejecting his final motion for a new trial.

Prosecutors argued Momeni stabbed Lee three times near the Bay Bridge following a dispute over his sister, Khazar Momeni, and her reported drug use. Video footage showed the two men leaving a Millennium Tower home together before the fatal altercation.

Momeni claimed self-defense, alleging Lee lunged at him with a knife while under the influence. Prosecutors told jurors this defense was "fabricated," and only Momeni's DNA was found on the knife's handle.

Lee's 18-year-old daughter, Scout Lee, addressed Momeni directly in court, saying "You did not just end his life, you ended an entire future built around a man." Family members described the proceedings as another tragic day.

Momeni's defense team vowed to appeal the conviction, while the case previously fueled a "doom loop" narrative about San Francisco street crime. The sentencing concludes a high-profile legal saga spanning over three years.
title: Tech consultant sentenced to 16 years to life in stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames continuing arrests as an aggressive “deportation offensive,” emphasizing Trump’s “misgivings,” hospital access blocked in a Latino neighborhood, and Venezuelan students detained; “unabated,” “rebuke,” and “wipeout” imply unchecked enforcement and voter rejection.

Right-Leaning coverage instead foregrounds Mullin’s “zero change,” executive authority, and roughly 3,600 daily deportations, presenting continuity as firmness while calling the GOP losses “crushing” or a “rout.” Center coverage bridges these views, stressing a “hardline” agenda and possible Latino voter backlash.
The pivotal divide is whether the election signaled repudiation or merely defeat; all agree arrests continued, Republicans lost heavily, and enforcement remained active.
summary: Despite Republican midterm losses, President Donald Trump intends to maintain his hardline immigration agenda, appointing Stephen Miller, architect of his deportation strategy, as his new White House chief of staff.
Exit polls show 57% of voters said Trump's enforcement has gone too far, yet Democrats won control of Congress, creating a divided government as the administration faces new oversight.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin vowed that "Deportations will continue" on all days including Thanksgiving and Christmas, while advocates reported arrests spanning Los Angeles, Phoenix, and Alabama.
The detention of an 8-year-old Haitian boy in San Diego and enforcement operations near a Los Angeles hospital sparked protests, with advocates calling the actions "state-inflicted trauma."

Democrats now possess subpoena power to investigate enforcement practices, detention conditions, and agency spending, giving Congress tools to demand accountability from the administration starting in January.
title: Mullin Vows No Change to Trump’s Immigration Policy Despite Republican Midterm Losses
topic_full: U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) · United States

bias: Left- and right-leaning coverage differs less ideologically than rhetorically: the left frames a “dramatic weather change” and “taste of winter,” while qualifying that snow in northwestern New Jersey may be minimal and highlighting freezing rain abroad.
The right emphasizes a “cold blast,” “wintry blast,” slick roads, travel disruption, and more than 110 million people potentially affected, portraying the storm as a broader threat.
Center coverage uses conditional language, stressing the east-west “major split” and coldest temperatures in six months.
All perspectives agree on rain, snow, colder air, and possible travel hazards, reflecting shared meteorological concerns rather than a clear partisan divide.
summary: A developing nor'easter is forecast to bring the season's first potential snowfall across the northeastern U.S. later this week, meteorologists predict.
The low-pressure system is expected to develop across the Ohio Valley later this week before moving toward the Mid-Atlantic by Friday, driven by a dip in the polar jet stream.
While major cities along the I-95 corridor expect cold rain, forecasters predict higher elevations across the Appalachians and interior Northeast could face snow risk between Thursday and Saturday.
Temperatures will turn noticeably colder beginning Friday, the FOX Forecast Center reported, with highs plummeting 20 degrees from Wednesday to Friday.
This cold blast should be relatively short-lived; NOAA's Climate Prediction Center forecasts a return to warmer-than-average temperatures across the East by next week.
title: First snow, coldest air in months headed for eastern US in wake of storm

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the Moscow–Dublin itinerary as “high-stakes” but necessary diplomacy, emphasizing continued peace efforts, mistrust between Putin and Zelensky, and the “significant” humanitarian value of a prisoner exchange.

Right-Leaning accounts portray Trump’s envoys as decisive, touting “significant progress” and a “biggest ever” release, while spotlighting territorial disputes and warning of “peace on Putin’s terms,” even calling them “controversial diplomatic envoys.” Center coverage de-emphasizes the exchange, stresses “no clear breakthrough,” and preserves uncertainty over the visit.
All agree the talks were “complex” and ongoing, reflecting broader divides over Trump’s diplomatic role, Russia’s leverage, and whether incremental humanitarian gains signal progress or risk.
summary: On November 10, US-mediated trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi yielded a large-scale prisoner exchange agreement between Ukraine and Russia following four hours of discussions between the delegations.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the initial Abu Dhabi discussions as productive, though he cautioned that a final settlement should not be expected within 24 hours.

Negotiators aim to "crystallize" decisions for Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, while Ukrainian Foreign Intelligence Service Chief Rustem Umerov outlined priorities including ending hostilities and securing postwar security guarantees.
White House Special Representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Kyiv and Moscow following the Abu Dhabi talks to hold direct discussions with the leaders.
Washington intends to expand the negotiation format to include European representatives directly, building on the established relationship with Putin and coordination with international partners.
title: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner may visit Russia in coming days, TASS reports

bias: Coverage largely converges on an arrest following a man’s reported bomb statement, but emphasis differs: left-leaning headlines use spare, chronological wording centered on “arrested” and “saying,” while right coverage similarly stresses authority, conduct, and arrest justification, including “acting irrationally,” without clearly partisan language.

Center reports add “allegedly” and “reports say,” tempering the alarming word “bomb,” while supplying logistical context: a United flight from Newark, safe landing, and passenger transfer—details de-emphasized elsewhere.
No perspective establishes that an explosive existed.
The shared focus on reported conduct and official intervention reflects broader tensions over threat perception, uncertainty, and institutional authority.
summary: On Monday, a United Airlines flight from Newark, New Jersey, landed safely at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport after a passenger allegedly claimed to have a bomb onboard.
Sheriff Joseph Lopinto said the 34-year-old man began acting irrationally around 11:20 p.m. and reportedly told crew members he possessed a bomb during the flight.
Carrying 46 passengers and six crew members, the Boeing 737 Max 9 arrived just before midnight, where all passengers were safely deplaned and transported to the terminal.
After being arrested without incident, the man was booked into Jefferson Parish Correctional Center on charges of communicating false information of planned arson and terrorizing.
The Federal Aviation Administration plans to investigate the incident, while Associated Press writer Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, contributed to this report.
title: A man is arrested after allegedly saying he had a bomb while aboard a flight bound for New Orleans
Five US states join FTC suit against Hims & Hers over privacy practices

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the 112 deaths— including 34 absent from official records—as migrant and refugee suffering enabled by institutional “under-reporting” and “impunity,” even invoking “scoundrel report” rhetoric.

Center coverage softens blame, describing deaths that “go undetected” and attributing the discrepancy to Oxford researchers, while right-leaning coverage stresses administrative breakdown through “no reliable public record,” foregrounding “foreigners” and adding that 44 deaths were suicides.
The pivotal divide is whether the episode signifies state accountability and humanitarian neglect or failed oversight and recordkeeping.
All perspectives emphasize inadequate healthcare, missing statistics, and custodial responsibility, reflecting broader disputes over migration, governance, and institutional trust.
summary: On Tuesday, Oxford University researchers reported that 112 foreign nationals have died in Greek police stations or migrant centers since 2000, documenting a 26-year pattern of custody-related fatalities.

The report's authors identified 'gaps in official police records and serious barriers to healthcare, including in facilities receiving European Union funding,' with 34 deaths documented by NGOs missing from official statistics.
Of the 112 deaths, 84 occurred in police stations without medical staff and 27 in migrant detention facilities, including a 37-year-old Pakistani man who died while detained in Athens.

The Council of Europe 's anti-torture committee, or CPT, cited persistent overcrowding in prison cells, including five detainees in spaces meant for one, with some sleeping on concrete or bedbug-infested mattresses.

Greece is currently implementing a 2025-2030 action plan to improve detention conditions and boost staff, aiming to protect prisoners' rights and address deficiencies researchers said could have been prevented.
title: Dozens of foreigners' deaths go undetected in Greece, Oxford University researchers say

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the case as “arbitrary detention,” saying Israel “refuses” release and is “neglecting” Abu Safiyah’s “deteriorating health,” while emphasizing weight loss, abnormal blood tests, the “unlawful combatants law,” and Gaza’s “severe shortage” of medical personnel.

The right-leaning presentation is narrower and more procedural, foregrounding the court ’s refusal to release 14 doctors and describing “health concerns” without broader allegations or medical detail.
A key dividing line is whether detention signals systemic harm to Gaza’s healthcare system or remains primarily a court decision.
Both emphasize the lack of charge or trial, denied examination, and rights-group concern, reflecting the Israeli-Palestinian legal and humanitarian divide.
summary: Israeli courts rejected petitions seeking the release of 14 Palestinian doctors from Gaza who are held without charges or trials.
The Lod District Court refused Dr. Hussam Abu Safia’s request for an independent medical examination and a second medical opinion.
Physicians for Human Rights Israel said Abu Safia had lost 14 kilograms, experienced falling hemoglobin levels, and had chest pain that was not properly investigated.
The group said the detentions further weaken Gaza’s healthcare system, which faces a severe shortage of medical workers after widespread infrastructure damage.
title: Israeli Court Refuses to Release 14 Gaza Doctors Held without Charge or Trial

bias: Left-Leaning coverage portrays Republicans as “sprinting” through a “judicial blitz,” stressing partisan haste, the broader backlog of 156 nominations, and 122 lacking committee votes, while noting 57 judges confirmed.

Right-Leaning coverage frames the same push as “unfinished business” against a “ticking clock,” defending Trump’s judicial legacy, abortion-related stakes, and warning of a Democratic “takeover,” while even calling insufficiently forceful Republicans “spineless, gutless wonders.” The center emphasizes a procedural “race” and explains Rudofsky’s withdrawal through Arkansas senators’ opposition.

All perspectives highlight the lame-duck deadline, pending judicial nominations, and Rudofsky’s replacement, reflecting deeper divides over institutional legitimacy, partisan power, and abortion policy.
summary: On Tuesday, President Donald Trump and Senate Republicans accelerated efforts to confirm judicial nominees before the Democratic majority assumes control next year.
Republicans aim to confirm 25 additional federal judges during the lame-duck session, building on the 57 federal judges already confirmed by this Congress.
President Trump formally named three new judicial nominees: Justice Department official Elliot Gaiser, Justice James Sullivan of the Texas Supreme Court, and William Grayson Lambert.

Following opposition from Arkansas Senators John Boozman and Tom Cotton, President Trump withdrew District Judge Lee Rudofsky's Eighth Circuit nomination on Tuesday, tapping Arkansas Supreme Court Justice Cody Hiland instead.

Confirming all pending nominees faces uncertainty as procedural requirements for home-state senator support and time constraints limit the legislative window before the Democratic majority takes control.
title: Senate Republicans kick off lame-duck dash to advance Trump judge picks

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the SEC’s roughly 25% decline as a Trump-era policy retreat, using “plunge” and skeptical scare quotes around “return to basics”; right-leaning coverage emphasizes measurable scale—348 actions versus 583, $1.10 billion ordered, and activity at its “lowest level since 1991”—while softening the picture by noting investor distributions “rose” to $731 million.
Center coverage, de-emphasized here, stresses penalties near $1 billion, the lowest since the 2008 crisis, and uses “plummets” without assigning policy intent.
The dividing line is whether reduced enforcement signals deregulation or recalibration; all acknowledge a sharp decline tied to Trump-era governance.
summary: On Tuesday, the Securities and Exchange Commission reported 348 enforcement actions in fiscal 2026, the fewest cases since 1991, following a record 43-day government shutdown and abrupt leadership changes.

Enforcement cases dropped about 25% during the first full fiscal year under President Donald Trump , reflecting a strategic shift from Biden-era enforcement priorities toward what leaders call a 'return to basics.'
The agency levied $343 million in civil penalties and $752 million in disgorgement, a fraction of the $7.2 billion ordered the prior year, which included a large Ponzi scheme judgment.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts expressed concern, stating Congress will scrutinize whether the agency is protecting the American people or working for Wall Street interests.
At a Fordham Law School event on Tuesday, New SEC Enforcement Director David Woodcock said "activity and effectiveness are not the same," adding he is "comfortable" with current staffing levels.
title: US SEC enforcement activity plunges two years into Trump administration

bias: The left presentation frames the initiative through the formal MOU and “ Taiwan Fellowship Program,” emphasizing language training, regional studies, and “bilateral strategic ties.” The right presentation foregrounds U.S. federal employees working in Taiwan offices, using the broader phrase “fellowship scheme” and “strengthen ties with Taipei,” while de-emphasizing educational details.
Neither uses overtly partisan terms such as “woke” or “crisis”; the key dividing line is study-oriented diplomacy versus practical government placement.
Center coverage bridges these frames, citing the de facto U.S. embassy and describing relations as “already close.” All portray the program as intended to deepen U.S.-Taiwan ties.
summary: On Tuesday, the United States and Taiwan signed a memorandum of understanding to launch the Taiwan Fellowship Program , allowing U.S. federal employees to receive up to one year of language training and regional studies in Taiwan.

Congress authorized the initiative under the Taiwan Fellowship Act, which President Joe Biden signed into law on Dec. 23, 2022, though the American Institute in Taiwan offered no explanation for the nearly three-year delay in implementation.
Participants will undergo intensive Mandarin training before working in Taiwan's government offices or agencies for up to one year, mirroring the 1994 Mike Mansfield Fellowship established for Japan.
AIT Managing Director Ingrid Larson stated the program "reflects strong bipartisan support for the U.S.-Taiwan relationship and a shared commitment to the people-to-people ties at its core."

Although the United States maintains no formal diplomatic ties with Chinese-claimed Taiwan, the initiative strengthens bilateral partnerships ahead of President Donald Trump's scheduled meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week.
title: US federal employees to work in Taiwan government offices under scheme to strengthen ties

bias: Left-Leaning coverage emphasizes how “stringent” U.S. controls failed to stop a military-linked university from obtaining restricted technology, while right-leaning accounts sharpen the security frame with “PLA-linked,” “blacklisted,” and “circumvent” language, implying deliberate evasion.
The right also stresses scale—two H200 chips costing $123,000 and assigned to a management school—tempering the threat with limited quantity.

Center coverage instead highlights “gaps” in Washington’s policy and scrutiny of Nvidia and Jensen Huang’s lobbying, while calling the chips “powerful.” All perspectives emphasize the purchase, military ties, restrictions, and procurement records, reflecting wider U.S.-China tensions over technology, security, and regulatory effectiveness.
summary: Northwestern Polytechnical University, a member of China's "Seven Sons of National Defense" group, purchased two Nvidia H200 chips for 874,700 yuan in October despite being on a U.S. export blacklist.

The U.S. Commerce Department added Northwestern Polytechnical to its Entity List in 2001; the university bypassed direct channels by acquiring the chips from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology, a domestic supplier.

Beihang University bought four A800 processors for 489,000 yuan in April, while Shenzhen University acquired three H100 processors for 769,800 yuan in September, illustrating widespread procurement across Chinese institutions.

Congressional leaders requested a briefing with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on November 18 over his lobbying efforts and alleged intelligence contacts amid the Trump administration's case-by-case export policy.

Despite Beijing withholding approval for large-scale imports, the H200 continues reaching China through indirect routes, providing essential capacity for training advanced AI systems according to recent reports.
title: PLA-linked Chinese university bought Nvidia H200 chips despite US blacklist: Reuters

bias: Left-Leaning coverage emphasizes that the ruling merely lets Trump’s defamation claim proceed, portraying “huge victory” and “terrible abuser of the truth” as his rhetoric rather than legal conclusions, while noting the unfair-trade claim’s dismissal.
Center coverage stresses procedure, the BBC ’s “strains credulity” response, and that no defamation was proven.
Right-Leaning coverage frames the decision as a “major legal victory,” labels the footage “deceptively edited,” and echoes “fake news,” while de-emphasizing the dismissed claim and BBC’s defense.
The pivotal divide is whether edited January 6 footage reflects deception or contested interpretation; all emphasize the multibillion-dollar stakes and ongoing Trump-media conflict.
summary: On Tuesday, U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Kuntz allowed President Donald Trump 's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC to proceed, though he dismissed the unfair trade practices claim against the broadcaster.

Trump sued after a 2024 BBC documentary spliced two segments of his 2021 speech, creating a false impression he incited the Capitol riot; the broadcaster apologized for the edit but denies defamation.
During the ongoing discovery phase, the BBC challenged the adequacy of Trump's document search, noting his privilege log contained only 20 items while theirs included 2,712 entries over 425 pages.
Magistrate Judge Enjolique A. Lett questioned the limited production size, while Trump declared the ruling a "huge victory," vowing to continue fighting those he claims deceive the American People.
The legal case hinges on whether Trump can establish "actual malice" by the BBC, as the court noted he must prove the broadcaster published statements knowing they were false.
title: US judge says Trump’s $10 billion BBC defamation case can proceed

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the case as a “grim discovery” transformed into a hopeful rescue, stressing the baby’s “clinging to life” condition and survival; right-leaning accounts intensify individual culpability, foregrounding the father’s alleged conduct, prior criminal history, and law-and-order implications through phrases like “horrific case,” “miraculously survives,” and “God is good.” Center coverage distinguishes allegation from adjudicated guilt with “believed” and “authorities said,” while detailing the multi-agency search.
The pivotal divide is whether to emphasize medical peril and rescue, or punishment and personal responsibility.
All perspectives highlight the 11-month-old found alive after roughly 24 hours underground, reflecting shared shock but contrasting humanitarian, institutional, and punitive priorities.
summary: On Tuesday, authorities in Lexington County found 11-month-old Koah Sharpe alive, roughly 24 hours after he went missing. Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said the infant was discovered buried in a shallow hole inside a dog crate.

Koah was taken by his father, Michael Comer, on Monday. A massive search involving nearly 100 officials ensued after deputies found the home empty, prompting collaboration with the FBI and other federal agencies.

Searchers located the site about 50 yards into woods near Comer's father's house. Koon noted the crate was wrapped in a towel, which "probably created an air pocket" that allowed Koah to survive the burial.

Late Monday, deputies arrested Comer on a burglary charge after finding him in a shed, though the infant was not present. The Lexington County Sheriff's Office is working with prosecutors on potential additional charges.

Court records reveal Comer was on probation following a guilty plea for aggravated breach of peace. He also faced previous arrests earlier this year for domestic violence and a weapons-related charge, according to state records.
title: Baby boy found alive in South Carolina after believed buried for 24 hours, police say

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds the human tragedy and uncertainty over intent, using terms like “tragedy” and “plows into” while stressing that investigators had not determined whether the collision was accidental or deliberate.

Right-Leaning coverage heightens shock and disorder with phrases such as “horrific collision,” “chaos erupted,” and “barrels into people,” while emphasizing the food stand, sidewalk impact, and possible hit-and-run implications.
Center coverage, where present, uses “crash” and “what we know” to organize verified details and emergency response.

All perspectives agree on three deaths, critical injuries, and an unresolved cause, reflecting shared attention to loss but differing instincts about emotional intensity, uncertainty, and public-safety implications.
summary: On Tuesday, a white SUV crashed into a food stand near the North Hollywood Metro Station, killing three people and injuring at least three others in critical condition.
The incident occurred shortly before 6 p.m. in the 5000 block of North Lankershim Boulevard, where a food stall typically serves commuters near the Metro station.

Aerials from AIR7 showed the white SUV stopped under a canopy amid scattered debris, while fire trucks and Los Angeles Police Department vehicles blocked the intersection during the emergency response.
Paramedics transported the critically injured to nearby hospitals while authorities closed surrounding streets to motorists, launching an investigation into the collision.
Circumstances of the crash remain unknown as the Los Angeles Police Department continues its investigation, and the driver's condition has not been disclosed.
title: At least 3 people dead after vehicle strikes pedestrians in North Hollywood, officials say

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Bessent’s remarks at a National Committee on U.S.-China Relations gala as a constructive push for “balanced” trade , reciprocity, and domestic job-creating production, while de-emphasizing geopolitical stakes.

Right-Leaning coverage casts China as a broader strategic challenge, invoking an “impetuous arms race,” “trade and investment offensive,” and “AI supremacy,” while portraying Taiwan as a “valuable ally.” Center coverage bridges them with “de-risk, not decouple,” “harbor no illusions,” and an AI incident channel.
All highlight Bessent’s trade concerns and the expected third Trump-Xi meeting that year, but only center and right stress managed rivalry alongside cooperation.
summary: On Tuesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the United States and China should harbor no illusions about their differences while navigating cooperation to mitigate Artificial Intelligence risks and compete for AI supremacy.

Bessent will travel to China next week for President Donald Trump's third meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, scheduled on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.

The summit will advance a bilateral dialogue on "superintelligence" to "prevent a misunderstanding between our two systems," Bessent said, with both sides agreeing to establish a direct alert channel for serious incidents.

$30 billion in mutual tariff cuts on non-sensitive goods forms part of a proposed Board of Trade , alongside a separate Board of Investment to provide increased predictability for companies operating in both nations.

Separately, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces an internal board investigation regarding an alleged relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset, though Nvidia stated no national security secrets were compromised.
title: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calls for more balanced US-China trade ties ahead of Trump-Xi talks

bias: The left-leaning framing presents a procedural “lawsuit” over absentee ballots, while right-leaning coverage sharpens the dispute into a campaign effort to obtain “rejected” ballot data and highlights a “quick” ruling, giving ballot administration greater prominence without overtly partisan language.
Center coverage supplies the most context, describing a list of voters whose ballots were rejected and calling the Senate race “closely watched,” a characterization de-emphasized elsewhere.
The pivotal divide is therefore specificity—absentee ballots generally versus access to rejected-ballot information—not competing claims about the case’s merits, which remain unexplored.
All perspectives emphasize that the judge expects to decide soon, reflecting shared focus on legal timing amid differing priorities.
summary: On Tuesday, Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews heard arguments in a lawsuit filed by Alaska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign seeking a list of absentee voters whose ballots were rejected.
The campaign sued Friday to ensure all qualified votes are counted, but attorneys for the State argued that releasing the requested lists would violate voter privacy laws.

Michaela Thompson, who manages absentee ballot review boards, stated the State's "old, inflexible" voter database cannot produce reports excluding confidential addresses that voters seek to keep private.
Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan's campaign filed a motion supporting the State's position, while Matthews plans to issue a written ruling within a day of Tuesday's hearing.
With the election too early to call, the Division of Elections targets Nov. 18 to finalize tabulations if no candidate wins more than 50% of first-choice votes.
title: Judge weighs lawsuit brought by Peltola campaign over absentee ballots in Alaska’s US Senate race

summary: On Monday, Flight UA2174 departed Newark International Airport for New Orleans when pilots transmitted a 7500 squawk code after a passenger announced he had a bomb and attempted to breach the cockpit.
Flight attendants de-escalated the situation by convincing the disruptive passenger to move to the rear of the aircraft, allowing the Boeing 737 MAX 9 to land safely in New Orleans without incident.

Aviation content creator Aaron Rheins confirmed the flight triggered a Level 4 alert indicating a cockpit breach attempt, with Air Traffic Control audio revealing the passenger "spoke nearly no English" while claiming to possess a bomb.
United Airlines confirmed that "law enforcement met the aircraft upon arrival" in New Orleans, where the passenger was arrested and booked into the Jefferson Parish Correctional Center.
The suspect faces charges of communicating false information of planned arson and terrorizing, and is currently held without bond by the Jefferson Parish Sheriff pending legal proceedings.
title: United Airlines Flight Issues Hijacking Alert After Passenger Claims to Have Bomb and Attempts to Enter Cockpit

summary: On Wednesday, Israeli airstrikes killed three Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, including two brothers, according to local health officials. Three more were killed Tuesday in a separate air attack on the Ghubain family home in Gaza City's Daraj area.
Violence persists despite last year's "ceasefire," with at least 1,600 Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks since the truce began. Hamas and Israel accuse each other of undermining the agreement.
A recent storm exacerbated the crisis, flooding about 70,000 tents in 12 hours and causing about $3m in damage. Displaced father Hisham Abdou said, "All the clothes are completely gone."
The Israeli military claims to be targeting militants in these areas but provided few details. Israel is blocking 60,000 mobile homes and 200,000 tents from entering Gaza.
More than 74,000 people have been killed in the war since October 7, 2023, according to ministry data. Little progress has been made on the eventual reconstruction of Gaza.
title: Israeli strikes kill three people including two brothers in Gaza, medics say

summary: On Sunday, a massive crowd of counter-protesters gathered in Rittenhouse Square, Philadelphia, to support Jewish-owned businesses targeted by a bike boycott organized by groups calling the restaurants "Zionist establishments."

A flyer circulating since October 30, 2026, promoted the boycott against six Jewish-owned eateries including Goldie and K'Far Cafe; critics condemned the timing, as the event fell on the 88th anniversary of Kristallnacht, the 1938 Nazi pogrom.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker condemned the targeting as antisemitism, while the businesses, owned by Michael Solomonov's group, faced scrutiny for prior fundraising of more than $100,000 for the Friends of United Hatzalah following the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.

The bike boycott effectively collapsed soon after starting as counter-demonstrators formed lines outside the targeted eateries; Philadelphia Police reported three arrests during the tense event, though no major physical altercations occurred.

Organizers have reportedly teased another event dubbed a "ride of return" slated for November 15, 2026, while community members emphasize the need for ongoing patronage rather than just a one-day surge.
title: Hundreds gather in Philadelphia for Pro-Palestinian demonstration and counterprotest

summary: On Tuesday, the Iraqi Civil Aviation Authority barred a plane carrying Iran's national soccer team from landing at Basra airport, citing potential violations of United States sanctions on Iranian airlines.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that airports servicing Iranian airlines face exclusion from the United States dollar system, a policy designed to ground Iran's civil fleet worldwide.

The Iranian team, traveling to participate in a tournament in Basra involving Iraq, Lebanon, and Palestine, returned to Abadan; officials confirmed the team will travel overland to complete the journey.

Iraq previously suspended Iranian flights to Baghdad in September following Washington's threats of secondary sanctions against service providers, demonstrating the escalating impact of these restrictions on regional aviation.
Intensified sanctions support President Donald Trump's goal to economically squeeze Iran as the United States and Israel continue the war launched in February.
title: Iraq bars plane carrying Iran's soccer team from landing in Basra over US sanctions, officials say

summary: On Tuesday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit vacated lower court orders restricting federal officers' use of tear gas and nonlethal munitions at the Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Portland.

Circuit Judge Kenneth Kiyul Lee wrote for the majority that agents need not wait until they face "an imminent threat of physical harm" to deploy nonlethal force, citing evidence officers were barricaded and targeted with lasers.

The appellate court rejected claims that federal agents violated First Amendment rights or constitutional liberty, describing protesters and REACH Community Development residents as "unfortunate collateral casualties" of federal crowd control efforts.

Dissenting in part, Circuit Judge Ana de Alba argued the court should have maintained prohibitions against firing munitions at heads or torsos, noting tenants met the standard of "shocking the conscience."

Although the preliminary injunctions ended, the underlying lawsuits remain active, and attorneys for REACH Community Development expressed disappointment, stating the ruling leaves residents without protection from chemical munitions deployed by federal agents.
title: Appeals court panel ends temporary ban on tear gas near Portland ICE building

summary: On Monday, U.S. District Court Judge Dena Coggins ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement to release UC Berkeley student Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez from detention, ending her weeklong confinement following her Oct. 31 arrest at San Francisco International Airport.

The 23-year-old business administration student was arrested while preparing to board a flight to Oregon; Department of Homeland Security officials claimed Albornoz Hernandez was deportable for overstaying her visa, though she maintains an active asylum case.

Attorneys for Albornoz Hernandez argued her detention without a hearing violated the U.S. Constitution, and Judge Coggins agreed, writing that "due process forbids the government from detaining the noncitizen" without adequate notice and a pre-deprivation hearing.

Celebrating the release, Berkeley Chancellor Richard Lyons stated, "Today, we celebrate this news and look forward to welcoming Paula back." Albornoz Hernandez is now reuniting with her boyfriend, Anthony, in Bakersfield.

While her asylum case remains pending, DHS criticized the ruling as coming from a "Biden-appointed activist judge" while stating the agency "complies with all lawful court orders." Albornoz Hernandez is preparing to return to her studies at Haas School of Business.
title: Judge orders UC Berkeley student released from ICE custody

summary: On Monday, District Judge David Nye sentenced Alexander Scott Mercurio, 21, to 18 years in federal prison for attempting to provide material support to ISIS and plotting to attack churches in Coeur dAlene, Idaho.

After Mercurio selected local churches for attack, the FBI arrested him on April 6, 2024, one day before planned strikes; he had pledged allegiance to the Islamic State, planning to use firearms, explosives, and knives.

Messages to the FBI revealed his intent to kill as many people as possible at one church, set it on fire, and continue elsewhere; agents discovered butane canisters, lighters, handcuffs, and his father's rifles.

Defense attorneys Carter Powers Beggs and Stephen Roberts described Mercurio as an isolated, depressed teen who has since renounced his extremist views, requesting a nine-year sentence rather than the 18 years imposed.

Following his prison term, Mercurio will face lifetime supervised release. Idaho U.S. Attorney John Shirts said the sentence "sends the clear message that where individuals intend to pursue acts of terrorism against the United States... they will be brought to justice .
title: An Idaho man gets 18 years in prison for an Islamic State support plot

summary: On Tuesday, The New York Times reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved from his home to a military base after Iranian threats against his life, citing sources with knowledge of the matter.
Bessent serves as the face of Washington's economic pressure campaign against Tehran during the US-Israeli war on Iran, which began on February 28, making him a primary target for retaliation.

A Trump administration intelligence memo warned late last month that lethal plots by Tehran against American citizens have reached "advanced stages," though officials noted Iran's ability to execute large-scale attacks in American territory remains limited.
Iran has consistently denied plotting to attack officials on American soil, while the Treasury Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment regarding Bessent's relocation.
The US-Israeli conflict continues to strain relations, having claimed top Iranian officials including the late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, contributing to the current threat environment.
title: US Treasury chief Bessent moved to military base after Iranian threats: Report

summary: On Tuesday, Rep. Jared Huffman, incoming chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee, issued letters demanding the Interior Department preserve all records and data relevant to President Donald Trump 's construction projects following whistleblower warnings of document destruction.

Multiple credible whistleblowers approached Huffman's committee in recent weeks to alert officials that the Interior Department was disposing of records before Democrats assumed control of Congress in January, prompting the preservation demand.

The Interior Department called the claims "100% false," stating it follows all federal records management obligations, while projects including the triumphal arch and East Potomac Golf Links are set to advance over the next 60 days.

Recipients of preservation letters sent to federal agencies and companies like Lockheed Martin must suspend deletion practices and certify compliance, with Huffman's committee prepared to issue subpoenas if the administration resists information requests.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said "President Trump is moving at lightning speed" because the administration has no time to waste, while Huffman signaled "it's just going to be an entirely new day" for congressional oversight with subpoena powers.
title: Whistleblowers tell Democrats documents linked to Trump’s construction projects are being destroyed

summary: Former President Joe Biden made a surprise visit to Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday to support his son, Hunter Biden, who received the Gold Medal for Outstanding Contribution for Public Discourse from The Hist.

Hunter was recognized for his advocacy on American politics and addiction recovery, joining past recipients including Irish President Michael Higgins and Bob Geldof. The award underscores his commendable contributions to public discourse.

Biden sat in the front row as Hunter recounted a family intervention during his struggle with addiction, drawing enthusiastic applause from the crowd when they noticed the former president in the hall.
As the family left the venue, objects including milk were thrown at the Bidens. Garda officers intervened, with at least two arrests made following the incident outside the college.

Earlier Tuesday, Biden met with Taoiseach Miche Martin while managing aggressive prostate cancer diagnosed last year. He has scaled back promotional appearances for his memoir "Promise Me, America," releasing November 17.
title: Pro-Palestinian protesters pelt objects at Joe Biden outside Irish university

summary: Democratic Rep. Doris Matsui won reelection in California's 7th Congressional District on Tuesday, defeating Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang with 55.8% of the vote.
Matsui has represented the Sacramento-area in Congress since winning a special election in 2005, succeeding her late husband, Robert Matsui, who served in Congress since 1979.
Vang posed the toughest challenge to Matsui in two decades; she finished ahead in the primary with 31% to 29%.
Following her victory, Matsui said voters chose the "steady solutions" she has delivered throughout her service as their representative.
While Matsui secured her seat, other California congressional races remained too close to call, including Rep. Mike Thompson's lead in the 4th District.
title: Democrat Doris Matsui wins reelection to U.S. House in California’s 7th Congressional District
